suite.doc: The IPv6-only IS-IS level-2 underlay: adjacencies on every core link, every loopback reachable, and enough MTU headroom for the SRv6 encapsulation.

suite.doc: BGP L3VPN over SRv6, per tenant: the route reflector has every PE as an established VPNv4 client and every data-centre LAN of every tenant; every PE imports the other LANs of a tenant into that tenant's VRF only, with an SRv6 SID from the right locator, and the kernel VRF carries them as seg6-encapsulated routes; every CE learns the other LANs of each tenant in that tenant's own VRF, over that VRF's eBGP session.

suite.name: 05 End To End

test.name: Every host pings every other host of its own tenant across the core

test.doc: Shut every client session on p1 (peer-group shutdown), wait for the PEs to drop it, then prove that every VRF still has every remote LAN (now with a single path, via the surviving reflector), that the SRv6 encapsulation routes are still in the kernel, and that every host still reaches its tenant peers.

suite.doc: Route-reflector redundancy: every PE holds each VPN route from every reflector; shutting the sessions of one reflector leaves every tenant working (routes and SIDs from the other), and the sessions come back once the reflector is restored. suite.doc: Explicit-path SRv6 steering (traffic engineering): a tenant prefix on pe1 is pinned to the path p1 -> p3 -> pe3 — the long way round the triangle — while the IGP shortest path stays p2. With uSID locators the whole path is ONE segment (the carrier <block>:<uN p1>:<uN p3>:<uN pe3>:<uDT4>::) and every hop shifts the destination address; with uncompressed locators it is a three-segment SRH. Captures prove the packets carry the path and transit p1/p3, that p2 never sees them, and that the return traffic keeps the shortest path.

suite.doc: Core link failure: the p2-pe3 link is cut silently (a firewall drop on p2's interface — carrier stays up, exactly like a UDP-tunnel link that has gone dead), BFD detects it in under a second, pe3 reroutes every tenant through p3, a continuous ping across the core loses at most a handful of packets, and everything returns to the shortest path once the link is restored. The suite always restores the link in its teardown.
